## Abstract

## Motivation

### The World of Sports

The world of sports is driven by excitement, unpredictability, limits of human skills. It pushes athletes to continously improve through practice sessions, training, and even competition:

-   [Soccer:]{.underline} Tests endurance, teamwork, and overall athleticism.

-   [American Football:]{.underline} Demands rapid reaction times, quick decision-making under pressure, and raw physical endurance.

-   [Golf:]{.underline} Challenges patience, spatial awareness, and precision physics.

As new sports are born, they introduce new ways to measure capabilities and innovations, Which leads to a motorsport that establishes these two qualities, Formula 1.

### Formula 1 History

Officially launched in 1950, (A Brief History of F1), Formula 1 has grown exponentially in global popularity. Over time, advancements in engineering alongside new circuits or renovated circuits have reshaped racing strategy and technical challenges.

### What is Formula 1?

Formula 1 is not soley a sport where a human is facing extreme gravity pushback, high speeds, heat physical dehydration; Formula 1 is also a sport of engineering. Each constructor must design a unique car within strict regulations. While the cars may look similar on the surface, their underlying engineering and aerodynamics vary significantly.

Additionally, Formula 1 not only make changes for the cars in the for every race, it also has led to some innovation that modern day drivers use. To list a few (RAWCA, Survana):

-   Steering-wheel-mounted vehicle controls

-   Push-button ignition systems

-   Advanced aerodynamic modeling to improve fuel efficiency and handling

### Reason for Analysis

With Formula 1's recent surge in popularity, I have become an avid viewer of the sport. With a particular incident during the 2026 Mexico Grand Prix weekend inspiring this analysis.

During qualifying, Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton secured pole position, while his teammate Charles Leclerc had qualified 3rd place, only a few milliseconds apart. Given that both drivers have the same engineered car adjusted to their driving prefences, which raises a key question: was that driver skill, slight difference between the two cars, or mere coincidence?

[![2026 F1 Mexico City Grand Prix - Qualifying Dashboard](images/clipboard-1624304035.png)](https://www.formula1.com/en/results/2026/races/1298/mexico/qualifying)

## Research Question

To what extent does car performance dictate the variance in driver championship points during Formula 1's turbo-hybrid era (2014–present)?

## Methodology

This analysis leverages the Jolpica API, an open-source data resource specifically dedicated to Formula 1. Which has been used to create a package for R called `f1dataR`.

Additionally, I will build two hand-coded .csv files covering season and regulation era, and season, constructor, and engine supplier, with both files joining the API data.

All raw data will be stored in a Github folder along with the other relevant files from this analysis.

### Data Source

-   [Jolpica API](https://github.com/jolpica/jolpica-f1)

-   [`f1dataR`](https://github.com/SCasanova/f1dataR)

## Data Preparation & Cleaning

### Data Extraction

#### Load in API Data

This will be a sample test to build up our .csv file for the analysis

Testing for one season is usually a good call to see how the rest of the data will be built and built together.

#### Test Build For a Season

[**Note:**]{.underline} Improvements will be made with challenges that come along pipeline

```{r getting 2014 data - test}
#| output: false
#| eval: false

clear_f1_cache() # Clears any past errors

# Get the schedule for a year
schedule_2014 <- load_schedule(season = 2014)
total_rounds  <- seq_len(nrow(schedule_2014))

# Create an empty list to store data
# This represents each racing weekend for that season
results_list <- list()

# For loop to fetch round sequentially
for (r in total_rounds) {
  df <- load_results(season = 2014, round = r)
  df$round <- r
  df$season <- 2014
  results_list[[r]] <- df
}

# Combine rows safely
results_2014 <- dplyr::bind_rows(results_list)
```

```{r printing 2014 data results}
glimpse(results_2014)
```

We can see that for one season we can gather all the necessary data we need along with including the round and what season it is in.

But this process of hard-coding the season and manually typing onto the R chunk makes this process a bit tedious. To improve on this task, we can create a function in R so we can tell the code to gather data for a particular season.

**Caution!** The 2026 season is still on-going so there may be a possible error as we try to gather data that may not exist, so we will implement try and catch blocks.

#### Building `get_season_function` Function

```{r get_season_function}
clear_f1_cache()

get_season_function <- function(season_year) {
  # Get the schedule for a year
  schedule_data <- load_schedule(season = season_year)
  total_rounds  <- seq_len(nrow(schedule_data))
  
  safe_load_results <- purrr::possibly(load_results, otherwise = NULL)
  
  # Create an empty list to store data
  # This represents each racing weekend for that season
  results_list <- list()
  
  # For loop to fetch round sequentially
  # Also placing round, season, and the df in a dataframe in the existing list
  for (r in total_rounds) {
    df <- safe_load_results(season = season_year, round = r)
    
    # Skip rounds that errored or came back empty (e.g. not raced yet)
    if (is.null(df) || nrow(df) == 0) {
      message("  No data for ", season_year, " round ", r, " - skipping")
      next
    }
    
    retrieved_at <- format(Sys.time(), tz = "UTC", usetz = TRUE)

    df <- df |>
      dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::everything(), as.character)) |>
      dplyr::mutate(
        season          = as.character(season_year),
        round           = as.character(r),
        retrieved_at    = retrieved_at,
        source_url      = paste0("https://api.jolpi.ca/ergast/f1/", season_year, "/", r, "/results.json"),
        f1dataR_version = as.character(utils::packageVersion("f1dataR")),
        .before = 1
      )
    
    results_list[[r]] <- df
    
    Sys.sleep(1.2)
  }
  
  if (length(results_list) == 0) return(NULL)
  
  return(dplyr::bind_rows(results_list))
}
```

#### Getting 2014-2026 Season Data

Now that we have built our function reproducing from our sample run of the 2014 data, we can now make the attempt to gather the data from the 2014 season to the data that currently exists so far for 2026. However if it is possible, as the 2026 season is coming to a close it is possible to extract the remaining rounds after the final race weekend on December 6th, 2026.

```{r testing season function}
test_2014 <- get_season_function(2014)
nrow(test_2014)
```

```{r getting 2014-2025 season data}
#| output: false
#| eval: false

# Clears past errors
clear_f1_cache()

# For data that doesn't exist yet as a precaution
safely_get_results <- purrr::possibly(get_season_function, otherwise = NULL)

# Targeting seasons and creating the list
years <- 2014:2026
season_list <- list()

# Loop over the years to extract data
for (year in years) {
  message("Processing Season: ", year, "")
  
  season_df <- tryCatch(
    get_season_function(year),
    error = function(e) {
      message("FAILED ", year, ": ", conditionMessage(e))
      NULL
    }
  )
  
  if (is.null(season_df)) {
    failed <- c(failed, year)
    next
  }
  readr::write_csv(season_df, paste0("results_", year, ".csv"))
  
  season_list[[as.character(year)]] <- season_df
  Sys.sleep(4.0)
}

# Create a new variable name for all rows of data
all_f1_season_list <- dplyr::bind_rows(season_list)
```

#### Qualifying Data

Now that we have extracted raw season data, we can now do the process of extracting the qualifying data.

```{r get_qualifying_function}
get_qualifying_function <- function(season_year) {
  schedule_data <- load_schedule(season = season_year)
  total_rounds  <- seq_len(nrow(schedule_data))

  # Protection at the round level, so one missing round can't wipe out a season
  safe_load_quali <- purrr::possibly(load_quali, otherwise = NULL)

  results_list <- list()

  for (r in total_rounds) {
    df <- safe_load_quali(season = season_year, round = r)

    # Skip rounds that give an error or is empty (such not raced yet)
    if (is.null(df) || nrow(df) == 0) {
      message("  No qualifying data for ", season_year, " round ", r, " - skipping")
      next
    }

    retrieved_at <- format(Sys.time(), tz = "UTC", usetz = TRUE)

    df <- df |>
      dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::everything(), as.character)) |>
      dplyr::mutate(
        season          = as.character(season_year),
        round           = as.character(r),
        retrieved_at    = retrieved_at,
        source_url      = paste0("https://api.jolpi.ca/ergast/f1/", season_year, "/", r, "/qualifying.json"),
        f1dataR_version = as.character(utils::packageVersion("f1dataR")),
        .before = 1
      )

    results_list[[r]] <- df
    Sys.sleep(1.2)
  }

  if (length(results_list) == 0) return(NULL)
  return(dplyr::bind_rows(results_list))
}
```

```{r testing qualifying function}
test_2014_qualifying <- get_qualifying_function(2014)
nrow(test_2014_qualifying)
```

### Data Cleaning

It may be easier to test the data cleaning on one year to then create a function to do this process on the remaining dataset for the seasons. With the same procedure for the qualifying data.

#### Data Clean Test Run

We will use the 2014 season to do a test run on what we need to clean for the remaining seasons and build a function out of that to automate the process.

```{r one season data cleaning}
season_raw_2014 <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaiderrX/CUNY-SPS-MSDS/refs/heads/main/DATA607/Projects/Final_Project/data/raw/season_raw/results_2014.csv")

head(season_raw_2014, 20)
glimpse(season_raw_2014)
```

Notes for seasons data cleaning:

-   We need our identifiers, the `driver_id`, and `constructor_id`

-   Race information: `round` and `season` is needed to identify the "when" in the data

-   We want to know when they start the race at their `grid` position

-   `laps` will assist in helping to see the `status` of the race

-   For `status`, this is the tricky part as we will need to categorize a status as "incident", "mechanical", or "other" due to various statuses existing in a Formula 1 race. With this idea, we can group them and map them as a categorical variable than a numerical variable

```{r testing data clean 2014}
cleaned_2014_season_data <- season_raw_2014 %>%
  select(season, round, driver_id, constructor_id, grid, position, points, laps, status) %>%
  mutate(
    status_clean = case_when(
      status == "Finished" | str_detect(status, "^\\+\\d+ Laps?") ~ "finished",
      status %in% c(
        "Brakes", "Clutch", "Drivetrain", "Electrical", "Electronics", 
        "Engine", "ERS", "Exhaust", "Gearbox", "Mechanical", "Oil leak", 
        "Oil pressure", "Power Unit", "Suspension", "Technical", "Turbo", 
        "Water leak", "Water pressure"
      ) ~ "mechanical",
      status %in% c(
        "Accident", "Collision", "Collision damage", "Rear wing"
      ) ~ "incident",
      TRUE ~ "other"
    )
  ) %>%
  select(-status) %>%
  rename(status = status_clean)
```

```{r examining cleaning test}
glimpse(cleaned_2014_season_data)
head(cleaned_2014_season_data, 10)
```

With the 2014 season cleaned, we can reproduce this process in a function for all of the season data.

#### Building `clean_season_function` function

```{r clean_season_function}
# We will list the types of statuses on here so it is easier to list in the function
mechanical_status <- c(
  "Brakes", "Clutch", "Drivetrain", "Electrical", "Electronics", "Engine",
  "ERS", "Exhaust", "Gearbox", "Hydraulics", "Mechanical", "Oil leak",
  "Oil pressure", "Power Unit", "Suspension", "Technical", "Turbo",
  "Water leak", "Water pressure", "Wheel", "Power loss", "Fuel system", "Transmission", "Tyre", "Throttle", "Brake duct", "Battery", "Overheating", "Wheel nut", "Vibrations", "Driveshaft", "Fuel pressure", "Seat", "Spark plugs", "Steering", "Out of fuel", "Radiator", "Cooling system", "Water pump", "Fuel leak", "Fuel pump", "Undertray", "Differential"
)
incident_status <- c(
  "Accident", "Collision", "Collision damage", "Damage", "Puncture",
  "Rear wing", "Spun off", "Front wing", "Debris"
)

# start of the function
clean_season_function <- function(raw_df) {
  clean <- raw_df |>
    select(season, round, driver_id, constructor_id, grid, position, points, laps, status) |>
    mutate(
      across(c(season, round, grid, position, points, laps), as.numeric),
      status_raw = status,
      status = case_when(
        status == "Finished" | status == "Lapped" | stringr::str_detect(status, "^\\+\\d+ Laps?") ~ "finished",
        status %in% mechanical_status ~ "mechanical",
        status %in% incident_status ~ "incident",
        TRUE ~ "other"
      )
    )
  
  # If there are other statuses that exist that are in the "other" mapping, we will see if it is there
  expected_other <- c("Retired", "Withdrew", "Disqualified", "Excluded", "Illness", "Did not start")
  unexpected_other <- clean |>
    dplyr::filter(status == "other", !status_raw %in% expected_other) |>
    dplyr::distinct(status_raw) |>
    dplyr::pull(status_raw)

  if (length(unexpected_other) > 0) {
    message("Unmapped statuses in 'other': ", paste(unexpected_other, collapse = ", "))
  }

  dplyr::select(clean, -status_raw)
}
```

#### Saving CSV files

Since it is tedious to save these files one by one, we can use `purrr`'s function to save it all instantly

```{r Saving clean seasons}
object_names <- c(paste0("season_cleaned_", 2014:2026), "all_seasons_cleaned")

# Put into a list
data_list <- mget(object_names, envir = .GlobalEnv)

# Use purrr's iwalk function to save all instantly
purrr::iwalk(data_list, ~ write_csv(.x, paste0(.y, ".csv")))
```
